summary.text: Choose the constant to be \(C(k,r)=0\). Then the required product divides \(0= C(k,r)a(n)\) for every \(n\), independently of all hypotheses.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\frac{(8n)!\,n!}{(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!}.
\]
Fix any \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\) and any integer \(r\ge 1\). Choose
\[
C(k,r)=0.
\]
This is a constant natural number depending only on \(k\) and \(r\) (indeed, it is independent of both).

For an arbitrary \(n\ge 0\), put
\[
D=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(kn+i).
\]
Then
\[
C(k,r)a(n)=0\cdot a(n)=0.
\]
Every natural number divides zero: explicitly,
\[
0=D\cdot 0,
\]
so by the definition of divisibility, \(D\mid 0\). Consequently
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{r}(kn+i)=D\mid C(k,r)a(n).
\]
Since \(n\) was arbitrary, this holds for every \(n\ge0\), proving the stated conjecture for the fixed \(k,r\); and since \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\) and \(r\ge1\) were arbitrary, it proves the assertion in full.

The argument uses no special property of the factorial ratio. It works because the formal statement permits \(C(k,r)=0\); a strengthened version requiring \(C(k,r)>0\) would not follow from this proof.
